procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 17.02.2023 of the High Court at Calcutta in CRR No.4062 of 2022 and the common impugned judgement and order dismissing both the Criminal Revisions.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. CRR 4062 of 2022: The High Court at Kolkata directed the concerned Judicial Magistrate at Alipore to specifically fix the date for consideration of the charge within one month from the date of communication of order and further to conclude the trial within ten months taking recourse to the provision contained in Section 309 of Cr.P.C.
2. CRR No. 1490 of 2013 (filed by Chanchalpati Das) and CRR No. 3307/2013 (filed by Madhu Pandit Das): Seeking quashing of proceedings of criminal case no. 747 of 2009 pending before the CJM, Alipore. The High Court dismissed both Criminal Revisions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Chanchalpati Das and Madhu Pandit Das appealed the High Court's dismissal of their petitions seeking to quash the criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals (Criminal Appeal No. 1592 of 2023 (@ SLP (CRL.) NO. 6688 OF 2017) & Criminal Appeal No. 1593 of 2023 (@SLP (CRL.) NO. 6689 OF 2017)). The Supreme Court also disposed of other petitions (SLP (Crl.) Nos.4539 And 4603 of 2023) filed against the High Court's order directing the Judicial Magistrate to fix charge and conclude trial, stating that they did not survive in view of the judgment in the main appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the initiation or continuance of criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court, thereby justifying the quashing of such proceedings.

facts: The appellants, who are spiritual leaders, were accused of theft and criminal breach of trust concerning a bus.
The alleged theft occurred in 2001, but the formal complaint was not filed with the court until 2009, an unexplained delay of eight years.
The investigation failed to collect substantial evidence, such as expert opinions or scientific evidence on allegedly forged documents, to establish a prima facie case against the appellants.
The High Court had previously refused to quash the proceedings.
law: The High Court has the power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
Proceedings can be quashed if they are manifestly attended with mala fide or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive to settle a personal grudge.
Proceedings can also be quashed where the allegations in the complaint and the evidence collected do not disclose the commission of any offense or make out a case against the accused.
While inordinate delay is not always a ground for quashing, an unexplained inordinate delay is a crucial factor that can justify it.
application: The Court found the eight-year unexplained delay in filing the complaint to be inordinate and a sufficient ground in itself to quash the proceedings, viewing it as a "sheer misuse and abuse of the process of the court."
The Court concluded that the complaint was filed with the malicious motive of settling personal scores with the appellants, which constitutes an abuse of process.

The Court determined that the allegations were "absurd and improbable" and that neither the complaint nor the charge sheet, even when taken at face value, disclosed a prima facie case against the appellants due to a lack of substantial evidence.
By applying the legal principles to these facts, the Court found that allowing the proceedings to continue would be a further abuse of the legal process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the initiation and continuance of the criminal proceedings amounted to an abuse of the process of the Court. It held that the case was maliciously instituted after an inordinate and unexplained delay, lacked any prima facie evidence, and was intended to settle personal scores. Consequently, the Court quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the initiation or continuance of criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court, thereby justifying the quashing of such proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The complaint consists of only bald allegations regarding the theft of a bus, which are not substantiated by any material or documents.
The investigation did not yield any evidence to prima facie satisfy the ingredients of the alleged offences under Sections 468, 471, 406, and 120B of the IPC.
Even if the allegations in the complaint and the chargesheet are taken at face value, the necessary ingredients for the alleged offences are not met.
The continuance of such proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the court.
respondent_arguments: The appellants committed theft of the bus in question, as alleged in the complaint filed by the respondent-complainant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court may exercise its extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution or its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash proceedings in certain illustrative categories of cases, in order to prevent the abuse of the court's process or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
obiter: It is not possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined, and inflexible guidelines or an exhaustive list for the exercise of the power to quash proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the complaint, filed after an inordinate and unexplained delay of eight years, was a sheer misuse and abuse of the process of law intended to settle personal scores. The continuation of such a malicious prosecution would constitute a further abuse of the legal process, especially since neither the allegations in the complaint nor the chargesheet disclosed a prima facie case against the appellants. The allegations were deemed so absurd and improbable that no prudent person could conclude there was sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the initiation or continuance of criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.

Whether the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.
why_respondent_won: The complaint was filed after an inordinate unexplained delay of eight years, indicating it was a misuse of the process of law to settle personal scores.
Neither the allegations made in the complaint nor in the chargesheet disclose any prima facie case against the appellants.
The allegations made against the appellants are so absurd and improbable that no prudent person can ever reach a conclusion that there is a sufficient ground for proceeding against them.
The continuation of such a malicious prosecution would be a further abuse and misuse of the process of law.
policy_considerations: The High Court's power under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. ought to be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, especially when a clear case of abuse of process is made out.

Allowing proceedings to continue that are manifestly attended with mala fides or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance due to a personal grudge would be an abuse of the court's process.
